title: A Gentle Answer and the LORD Who Sees
summary: The chapter opens with a gentle answer that turns away wrath and keeps returning to the tongue: soothing or perverse, timely or rash. Alongside speech it sets the LORD, who sees every place, weighs sacrifice and prayer, knows the depths of Sheol and of the human heart, and defends the widow's boundaries. Two better-than sayings prize a little with love and the fear of the LORD over plenty with turmoil, and the final verse joins the fear of the LORD to humility.
story: Chapter 15 closes the first half of the Solomonic collection. Many scholars see a change after this chapter: from 10:1 to 15:33 most sayings are contrasts joined by but, while from 16:1 onward the forms become more varied and the LORD and the king move to the center. This chapter already leans that way. The LORD is named nine times, more than in any chapter so far, and verse 33, which links the fear of the LORD with instruction and humility, forms a hinge into the concentrated sayings about God's rule that open chapter 16.
historical:
Verse 8 assumes Israel's system of worship, with sacrifices offered at the temple in Jerusalem (and, in earlier periods, at other sanctuaries). Proverbs rarely mentions the cult, but when it does, it agrees with the prophets: worship offered by people whose lives are unjust is detestable to God. Amos, Isaiah, and Micah, prophets of the eighth century BC, all made this point (Amos 5:21-24; Isaiah 1:11-17; Micah 6:6-8), as had Samuel much earlier (1 Samuel 15:22). The sage and the prophet speak with one voice.

Verse 25 alludes to a real legal vulnerability. Widows had no husband to defend the family's land in the gate, and property boundaries were marked by stones that could be quietly moved. The law cursed anyone who moved a neighbor's boundary marker (Deuteronomy 19:14; 27:17), and the prophets condemned those who seized fields. Proverbs says the LORD himself guards the widow's boundary.
cultural:
Verse 11 mentions Sheol and Abaddon. Sheol was the Hebrew name for the realm of the dead, pictured as a place below the earth where all the dead go, silent and shadowy. Abaddon, from a root meaning to perish, is a poetic name for the same place or for its deepest part (compare Job 26:6). If even these hidden depths lie open before the LORD, the saying argues, how much more the human heart. Verse 24 uses the same picture: the wise take the path that leads upward, away from going down to Sheol.

Verse 17 contrasts a dish of vegetables with a fattened ox. Most people in ancient Israel rarely ate meat, which was reserved for feasts, sacrifices, and the tables of the wealthy. A stall-fed ox was the food of kings (1 Kings 4:23). The saying chooses the peasant's plate with love over the banquet with hatred, which would have been a striking choice to anyone who seldom tasted beef.
literary: The chapter opens and closes with clusters on speech and correction. Verses 1 to 4 concern the tongue; verses 5 to 12 alternate between correction and the LORD's judgments; verses 13 to 17 turn to the heart and include two better-than sayings (verses 16-17), a form that sets two goods side by side and chooses the lesser one because of what comes with it. Verses 18 to 23 move between temper, work, family, counsel, and the joy of a fitting word. Verses 25 to 29 form the densest LORD cluster so far, four sayings about what the LORD tears down, detests, and hears. Verse 30 onward returns to cheer, reproof, and humility, ending on a line repeated in 18:12: “humility comes before honor.” Verse 11 uses a how-much-more argument, reasoning from the greater to the lesser.

outline.t: The gentle answer and the healing tongue
Correction, sacrifice, prayer, and the LORD who sees
The cheerful heart and the better-than sayings
Temper, counsel, a timely word, and the upward path
What the LORD tears down, detests, and hears
Good news, reproof, and humility before honor

doctrines.note: The LORD's eyes are in every place (verse 3), and Sheol and the human heart lie open before him (verse 11). His knowledge is complete, and it is not neutral: he watches the evil and the good, and he hears the prayer of the righteous (verse 29).

The prayer of the upright is his delight (verse 8), and he hears the prayer of the righteous (verse 29). Prayer is set above sacrifice offered without righteousness, and the heart behind worship is what God weighs.
The fear of the LORD is the instruction of wisdom (verse 33). Wisdom here includes timing (verse 23), gentleness (verse 1), and the willingness to hear life-giving reproof (verse 31).

words.note: Sheol, the realm of the dead. In the Old Testament it is the place of all the dead, not a place of punishment in the later sense of hell, though it is always a place of loss, far from the praise of God (Psalm 6:5). Later Scripture develops fuller hope beyond death. Here it serves to show that nothing is hidden from the LORD.

Anavah, humility. The word is related to anav, one who is lowly or afflicted, and it describes a person who knows his place before God and does not grasp for status. Verse 33 says humility comes before honor, reversing the usual human assumption that honor must be seized.

Zevach, sacrifice, especially the slaughtered offerings whose meat was partly eaten by the worshipers in a shared meal. Verse 8 says the sacrifice of the wicked is detestable to the LORD. The problem is not the ritual but the life of the one offering it.

Lev, heart, used nine times in this chapter. In Hebrew thought the heart is less the seat of feeling than the center of the person: thought, will, intention, and desire together. Verse 11 says the LORD sees it more easily than Sheol, and verse 28 shows the righteous heart pondering before it speaks.

christ: The New Testament letter of James reads almost like a Christian commentary on this chapter: be slow to speak and slow to anger (James 1:19), the tongue that blesses and curses (James 3), and God's opposition to the proud and grace to the humble. Jesus taught that reconciliation with a brother comes before an offering at the altar (Matthew 5:23-24), the same principle as verse 8. His parable of the Pharisee and the tax collector (Luke 18:9-14) turns on verse 33's claim that humility comes before honor. And Jesus described himself as gentle and humble in heart (Matthew 11:29), the very person whose gentle answer turns away wrath. These links are thematic, not predictive, but they show that the God who hears the prayer of the upright in Proverbs is the God Jesus taught his disciples to call Father.

hard.q: Does God refuse to hear the prayers of some people (verses 8 and 29)?
hard.a:
The verses say the sacrifice of the wicked is detestable to the LORD and that he is far from the wicked but hears the righteous. Read against the rest of Scripture, their target is worship that tries to use God while refusing to turn from evil. Isaiah heard the same message: God would not listen to the prayers of people whose hands were full of blood, yet in the same chapter he invited them to come and be cleansed (Isaiah 1:15-18). The wicked in Proverbs are those who persist in wrongdoing, not those who cry out for mercy.

The Bible is full of sinners whose prayers God heard when they turned: the tax collector in Jesus' parable, King Manasseh in 2 Chronicles 33, the city of Nineveh in Jonah. So these sayings do not describe a God who ignores repentance; they describe a God who cannot be bought with religious performance. Christian theology has always held both truths together: no one is righteous enough to demand a hearing, and no one who turns to God in need is turned away.

questions: Verse 1 promises that a gentle answer turns away wrath. Think of a recent conflict: what would a gentle answer have sounded like?
Verses 16 and 17 prefer little with love to plenty with turmoil. What would you give up to have more peace in your home?
Verse 11 says the heart lies open before the LORD. How does it feel to be fully known, and what difference does it make that the one who knows is also the one who hears prayer?
